solutions.latex:
$V_S=\dfrac43\pi R^3$ and $V_C=\dfrac13\pi\left(2h^2R-h^3\right)$.

$$\dfrac{dV_C}{dh}=\dfrac13\pi\left(4Rh-3h^2\right),\qquad\dfrac{d^2V_C}{dh^2}=\dfrac13\pi(4R-6h)$$

Let $\dfrac{dV_C}{dh}=0$:

$$\begin{aligned}4Rh-3h^2&=0\\ h\left(h-\dfrac{4R}{3}\right)&=0\end{aligned}$$

$h=0$ (not a solution, $h>0$) or $h=\dfrac{4R}{3}$.

When $h=\dfrac{4R}{3}$: $\dfrac{d^2V_C}{dh^2}=\dfrac13\pi\left(4R-6\left(\dfrac{4R}{3}\right)\right)=\dfrac13\pi(4R-8R)=-\dfrac{4\pi R}{3}<0$ since $R>0$, so there is a maximum at $h=\dfrac{4R}{3}$.

For maximum volume, $h=\dfrac{4R}{3}$:

$$\begin{aligned}V_C&=\dfrac13\pi\left(2R\left(\dfrac{4R}{3}\right)^2-\left(\dfrac{4R}{3}\right)^3\right)\\ &=\dfrac13\pi\left(\dfrac{32R^3}{9}-\dfrac{64R^3}{27}\right)\\ &=\dfrac13\pi\left(\dfrac{96R^3-64R^3}{27}\right)\\ &=\dfrac13\pi\left(\dfrac{32R^3}{27}\right)\\ &=\dfrac{32\pi R^3}{81}\end{aligned}$$

$$V_C:V_S=\dfrac{32\pi R^3}{81}\times\dfrac{3}{4\pi R^3}=\dfrac{8}{27}$$

Therefore the volume of the largest cone is $\dfrac{8}{27}$ of the volume of the sphere.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=2\int_{-3}^{-1}\sqrt{2x+6}\,dx+\int_{-1}^{5}\left(\sqrt{2x+6}-(x-1)\right)dx\\ &=2\int_{-3}^{-1}(2x+6)^{\frac12}dx+\int_{-1}^{5}(2x+6)^{\frac12}-x+1\,dx\\ &=2\cdot\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac23(2x+6)^{\frac32}\Big]_{-3}^{-1}+\left[\dfrac13(2x+6)^{\frac32}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}+x\right]_{-1}^{5}\\ &=\left[\dfrac23(4)^{\frac32}-\dfrac23(0)\right]+\left[\left(\dfrac13(16)^{\frac32}-\dfrac{25}{2}+5\right)-\left(\dfrac13(4)^{\frac32}-\dfrac12-1\right)\right]\\ &=18\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\int_{-2}^{4}(y+1)-\left(\dfrac{y^2}{2}-3\right)dy\\ &=\int_{-2}^{4}y-\dfrac{y^2}{2}+4\,dy\\ &=\left[\dfrac{y^2}{2}-\dfrac{y^3}{6}+4y\right]_{-2}^{4}\\ &=\left[\dfrac{4^2}{2}-\dfrac{4^3}{6}+4(4)\right]-\left[\dfrac{(-2)^2}{2}-\dfrac{(-2)^3}{6}+4(-2)\right]\\ &=\left[8-\dfrac{32}{3}+16\right]-\left[2+\dfrac86-8\right]\\ &=\dfrac{40}{3}+\dfrac{14}{3}=\dfrac{54}{3}=18\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\log_2(2-2x)&=\log_{\sqrt2}(1-x)\\ \dfrac{\ln(2-2x)}{\ln2}&=\dfrac{\ln(1-x)}{\ln\sqrt2}=\dfrac{\ln(1-x)}{\frac12\ln2}=\dfrac{2\ln(1-x)}{\ln2}\\ \ln(2-2x)&=2\ln(1-x)\\ 2-2x&=(1-x)^2\\ 2-2x&=1-2x+x^2\\ 1&=x^2\\ x&=\pm1\end{aligned}$$

Testing each value of $x$: the only solution is $x=-1$.

Method 2: let $y=\log_2(2-2x)$ and $y=\log_{\sqrt2}(1-x)$. Then $2-2x=2^y$, so $1-x=2^{y-1}$; and $1-x=\sqrt2^{\,y}=2^{\frac12y}$. Equating, $2^{y-1}=2^{\frac12y}$, so $y-1=\dfrac12y$ and $y=2$. Substituting into $1-x=2^{y-1}$: $1-x=2$, so $x=-1$.

solutions.latex:
The initial position of the particle is $x=4$. The only time the particle is at rest is when $t=\dfrac12$. At this time the displacement is

$$x=4+3\left(\dfrac12\right)e^{-2\left(\frac12\right)}=4+\dfrac{3}{2e}$$

In the limit as $t\to\infty$, $x=4+\dfrac{3t}{e^{2t}}\to4+0=4$.

Therefore the particle starts at $x=4$, travels right to $x=4+\dfrac{3}{2e}$, then travels left back to $x=4$ without ever reaching it.

The distance travelled when moving right is $\left(4+\dfrac{3}{2e}\right)-4=\dfrac{3}{2e}$. The distance travelled when moving left is also $\left(4+\dfrac{3}{2e}\right)-4=\dfrac{3}{2e}$. It follows that the greatest total distance is

$$\dfrac{3}{2e}+\dfrac{3}{2e}=\dfrac3e\text{ metres}$$
